title: VodafoneThree mulls UK–Norway subsea cable
snippet: VodafoneThree today announced a feasibility study into a new UK-Norway digital corridor The post VodafoneThree mulls UK–Norway subsea cable appeared first on Total Telecom.
fullText:
Press Release

VodafoneThree today announced a feasibility study into a new UK-Norway digital corridor, exploring a high-speed subsea cable route linking mainland Scotland to Shetland and onward to Norway.

The proposed route could deliver up to £8.2 billion in economic value over the next ten years*, according to research conducted by consultancy firm WPI Strategy and commissioned by Vodafone Business.

The proposed corridor could strengthen the security, resilience and capacity of the UK’s digital infrastructure, supporting defence, critical national infrastructure and essential services. Analysis commissioned by VodafoneThree estimates it could protect up to £6.6 million of UK economic activity for each day of severe disruption affecting multiple existing routes where traffic cannot be rerouted. This highlights the value of geographically diverse subsea infrastructure: an alternative northern route could bolster resilience as government identifies coordinated disruption to critical undersea infrastructure as a growing national security risk.

Expected to begin in summer 2027, the study will assess the Scotland-Shetland-Norway route and examine how greater international connectivity could support businesses, public services, defence, data centres and critical national infrastructure (CNI).

By providing additional high-capacity, resilient connectivity, the cable could help make northern Scotland and Shetland more attractive locations for data-centre investment. This could unlock wider economic benefits through construction, skilled employment, local supply chains and new commercial opportunities, subject to the findings of the feasibility study. It could also strengthen the case for investment in northern Scotland and Shetland, supporting regional growth, skilled employment and local supply chains.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting MP said: “Protecting our network of undersea cables is vital to keeping our country safe. Our adversaries are increasingly targeting our critical national infrastructure, including the cables that carry data and enable internet traffic and financial transactions.

“This is a very welcome step that could not only improve connectivity and boost our economy, especially in Scotland, but strengthen the UK’s national resilience, prevent disruption, and keep us all safe.”

Nick Gliddon, Business Director, VodafoneThree, said: “Reliable international connectivity is vital to the UK’s defence, strengthening our resilience to disruption and enhancing the security of the critical infrastructure on which our economy and public services depend. Norway is a strategically important partner, with a shared commitment to protecting infrastructure across the North Atlantic.

“A new digital corridor would strengthen the physical links between our countries, add vital route diversity and support secure, resilient connectivity for critical infrastructure on both sides of the North Sea. It could also unlock investment in data centres and AI, creating skilled jobs and wider economic opportunities. This study will help establish the economic and strategic case for the route and identify the partnerships needed to deliver it.”

The announcement builds on VodafoneThree’s now-completed feasibility study into a high-speed subsea cable connecting Shetland with mainland Scotland. For Shetland, a separate cable route could provide vital resilience where connectivity currently depends on a single cable system, with outages in 2022 and 2025 exposing the lack of an effective alternative when it fails.

The new study will identify potential routes from Shetland to Norway, as well as possible landing points and delivery partners in the Bergen region. Extending the route to Norway could improve connectivity for island communities and businesses, add resilience for Shetland Spaceport and other strategically important sites, and support future economic opportunities, including potential data-centre development.

VodafoneThree’s £11 billion network investment will support up to 13,000 jobs at the peak of its 5G Standalone (SA) network build. A new UK-Norway subsea cable via Shetland would help extend the benefits of that investment to the islands, supporting next-generation connectivity, unlocking wider economic opportunities and strengthening the resilience of critical digital infrastructure.

Strengthening digital security and resilience

Subsea cables carry 98% of international data traffic and are essential to modern economies. Damage or disruption can affect businesses, public services and organisations that depend on continuous access to digital services.

VodafoneThree will examine how a new route from mainland Scotland to Shetland and onwards to Norway could increase route diversity, support the secure movement of data and help defence, data centres, telecommunications networks and other CNI maintain essential services during disruption.

Building a stronger digital corridor between the UK and Norway

The study comes amid deepening UK-Norway cooperation on defence, security, energy and critical infrastructure. In December 2024, the two countries agreed a strategic partnership covering defence and security, energy and the green transition, alongside closer cooperation to protect subsea and offshore infrastructure across the North Atlantic.

The proposed digital corridor would explore a complementary opportunity to strengthen the infrastructure connecting the two countries. VodafoneThree wants to build the commercial partnerships needed to make the route viable, bringing together UK and Norwegian expertise across telecommunications, data centres, technology and infrastructure. These partnerships could support cross-border investment, innovation and skilled employment while improving the long-term resilience of essential digital and defence-related services.

Norway is emerging as a major location for AI data-centre investment, supported by its abundant renewable hydropower and cooler climate, which can reduce the energy required for cooling. A new direct link to Scotland would provide additional international route diversity and strengthen the resilience of Norway’s digital infrastructure, while creating new capacity to support the country’s growing AI economy. It would also be the first new direct subsea cable between Scotland and Norway in around a quarter of a century.

title: Arelion expands its ‘AI superhighway’ in the USA
snippet: Arelion today announced the expansion of its North American network with five new Points-of-Presence (PoPs) in key regional data center markets, extending the company’s AI superhighway The post Arelion expands its ‘AI superhighway’ in the USA appeared first on Total Telecom.
fullText:
Press Release

Arelion today announced the expansion of its North American network with five new Points-of-Presence (PoPs) in key regional data center markets, extending the company’s AI superhighway to a growing ecosystem of neocloud and GPU-focused compute campuses. These PoPs provide enterprise, neocloud, hyperscale and wholesale customers with high-capacity, diverse connectivity and rapid service delivery, supporting continued AI infrastructure growth.

The expansion brings connectivity to emerging GPU infrastructure markets in Reno and Fargo; major hyperscale and enterprise markets in Atlanta and Houston; and South Florida, where Miami supports both growing regional compute demand and subsea connectivity to Latin America and the Caribbean.

“We’re seeing significant customer demand in these regions as AI infrastructure expands beyond established data center hubs, with neoclouds and GPU-focused providers bringing compute capacity into new markets,” said Art Kazmierczak, Director of Strategic Sales and Network Development at Arelion. “Our North American AI superhighway gives these providers the capacity, diversity and speed-to-deployment they need to bring services online quickly, while enabling enterprises and cloud users to move large AI data sets and workloads between their networks, cloud environments and distributed GPU resources.”

Arelion provides IP Transit, 400G EVPL Ethernet, Wavelengths, Managed Optical Fiber Network (MOFN) services and more to serve these demands. These solutions enable terabit-scale connectivity and multiple paths for customers moving large data sets between GPU clusters and related digital infrastructure.

Demand for neocloud and AI infrastructure is expected to grow significantly, with Structure Research estimating that the global neocloud and AI infrastructure market will reach $186 billion by 2030 as critical IT capacity scales from approximately 2.3 GW to 150 GW.

Through its existing North American backbone, relationships with regional infrastructure providers and targeted new network construction, Arelion can rapidly extend high-capacity connectivity to emerging compute campuses. This agile deployment model enables neocloud providers to bring services online quickly while giving enterprises and other cloud users low-latency access to the GPU infrastructure required for compute-intensive AI workloads.

For enterprises, this expansion reduces latency and improves redundancy when moving workloads between on-premises infrastructure, cloud environments, and distributed GPU resources, without requiring direct investment in regional buildout.

As these requirements evolve across industries including financial services, biotech, energy and manufacturing, Arelion provides the scalable connectivity needed for AI model development, inference and other compute-intensive applications.

Extending Arelion’s AI superhighway into five regional compute markets:

Reno, Nevada – A new PoP extends Arelion’s AI superhighway into a growing GPU compute and hyperscale capacity market, with two locations supporting greater network diversity.

Fargo, North Dakota – A new PoP expands Arelion’s network to large-scale infrastructure supporting GPU and high-performance computing workloads.

Houston, Texas – A new PoP extends Arelion’s network in a major technology and energy market, supporting demand for AI and other data-intensive applications.

Atlanta, Georgia – A new PoP expands Arelion’s footprint in one of North America’s largest data center markets, supporting continued hyperscale and AI infrastructure growth.

Miami, Florida – A new PoP strengthens Arelion’s South Florida footprint, supporting regional compute demand and connectivity between North American networks and subsea systems serving Latin America and the Caribbean.

title: Smarter NOC management in the age of AI
snippet: We caught up with co-founder, CTO and CEO of ITcare, Andrian Visnevschi, to discuss scaling operations and the elusive nature of building autonomous networks The post Smarter NOC management in the age of AI appeared first on Total Telecom.
fullText:
Interview

We caught up with co-founder, CTO and CEO of ITcare, Andrian Visnevschi, to discuss scaling operations and the elusive nature of building autonomous networks

The UK’s fibre sector has a diverse and increasingly complex approach to network operations management. The largest fibre network players can afford to run 24/7 network operations centres (NOCs), manned by specialists to provide round-the-clock monitoring, fault management, and service assurance.

For the smaller players, however, the cost of a 24/7 NOC is often prohibitive, making alternative operational models more attractive. In some cases, this means network oversight by junior staff, or simply an automated alert sent to an on-call engineer, neither of which guarantees a fast response.

As Andrian Visnevschi, co-founder, CTO and CEO of ITcare, explained to us, this can result in costly delays.

“A lot of operators today simply don’t have 24/7 coverage. In some cases, senior NOC engineers are working a typical 9–5. If something happens outside of business hours, in the best case a more junior colleague calls them. Often, it’s just an automated notification from PagerDuty or a similar tool, which can easily be missed or ignored,” said Andrian. “Then the engineer has to wake up, or get home, or pull over the car, acknowledge the alert, find a stable internet connection, connect to the network, and only then start troubleshooting. That’s not a fast reaction. In fact, the mean time to repair of those issues is rising and the customers are suffering.”

Delays in fault repair cause significant damage to customer relationships and undermine the commercial value of the network – both factors of crucial importance in the UK’s highly competitive environment.

“A lot of operators are struggling to survive in the new race for service quality,” said Andrian, highlighting a recent market shift from network coverage to service take-up and reliability. “There is huge pressure to provide quality services without operational costs rising sky high.”

This is where ITcare’s model differs. Rather than a service desk that watches dashboards and escalates, ITcare’s NOC is staffed around the clock by senior network engineers who work across multi-vendor environments, from fibre ISPs and wireless operators to data centre fabrics, and resolve incidents themselves.

“A real NOC isn’t a service desk. The engineers on shift can log into the device, find the problem and fix it at 3am, without waking anyone up,” said Andrian. “They treat our customers’ networks as if they were their own. Every NOC customer we have signed is still with us today.”

HORA: The whole network in one view 

For ITcare, which runs managed NOC and network engineering services for telecoms customers, the first step to improvement is a unification of systems and data. Inventory mistakes, poor data visibility, and unclear network topology are commonplace, making resolving issues a slow, complex process. This was one of the primary reasons for the creation of HORA, ITcare’s AI network operations platform, which gives NOC engineers full visibility of the network in one place: inventory and source of truth, metrics, logs, traffic flows, BGP monitoring, live network state, configuration backups and controlled change management, with AI correlating across all of it. ITcare built it for its own NOC first, and its engineers use it every day on live customer networks.

“By combining all of the available data, HORA can quickly troubleshoot and provide root cause analysis. It can also show exactly which customers are affected by a specific outage,” said Andrian. “With all the network data in one place, engineers stop jumping between five different tools. That makes them far more efficient, lets us automate more of the routine work, and cuts response times.”

HORA is designed to be slotted over the top of the network, being on-prem by design and network management system-agnostic. All networks are different – Andrian talks of “fine tuning” HORA to each customer – but fundamentally there are many NOC processes that are similar, regardless of tech stack.

“Over the years, we’ve worked with different ISPs, cloud hosting providers, and data centres worldwide, and our engineers are often doing the same repetitive tasks with each. They may use different hardware, different network architecture, and different protocols, but the troubleshooting chain they all use on a daily basis is usually quite similar,” said Andrian. “That’s where AI can be useful. We’re able to automate some of these tasks to make engineers’ lives easier.”

In ITcare’s own NOC, HORA has cut median investigation time from around 28 minutes to under four, roughly seven times faster than manual root cause analysis.

HORA’s change management capabilities also mean that changes are clearly documented.

“Engineers are usually pretty lazy,” Andrian joked. “They like making changes but they don’t like updating the documentation. HORA not only creates a change management process for you to approve but also handles the documentation so it is always up to date.”

AI guardrails, and Autonomous Level 4

Despite being bullish on the benefits of AI integration, Andrian is no AI evangelist, describing ITcare in a previous Total Telecom article as “conservative in a specific way”. HORA underwent extensive testing in the company’s own NOC before being offered to customers, with strict guardrails in place.

“We’ve all heard horror stories about AIs connecting to data bases, erasing all the data, and even generating random data to replace it,” he said. “You’ve got to be really careful when you build these tools. In HORA, the AI can propose a change, but an engineer reviews and approves it. Nothing touches a device without that approval.”

These safety concerns are, at least in part, why attempting to rapidly progress to Level 4 (L4) autonomy – in which an AI system monitors the network and handles tasks without human intervention – could be highly dangerous.

“I think [many in the industry] are all rushing it too much. It’s really so complicated to reach L4,” said Andrian. “If you’re building something solely for your own operations and infrastructure then it may be possible. But as soon as something changes in the design or a new vendor is added, you’ll need to start again.”

Keeping expert humans in the loop

For Andrian, the use of AI in NOC management is not about replacing engineers, but rather enhancing their abilities so networks can be scaled effectively without expanding overheads.

“It’s about allowing you to scale easily. With HORA, a single engineer has a tool that can quickly get to root cause, assess the impact, and prepare a change across hundreds of devices from a plain-language request, which the engineer then reviews and approves,” said Andrian.

“The tool doesn’t replace the engineer. Our customers get senior engineers on shift around the clock, and HORA makes each of them faster,” he added.

For operators under pressure to improve service quality while controlling costs, the immediate opportunity lies in pairing experienced engineers, whether in-house or through a partner, with tools that let them work smarter and scale operations more efficiently. Full autonomy remains a longer-term ambition.

Andrian Visnevschi is CEO and CTO of ITcare and holds JNCIE-SP #2975. ITcare runs managed NOC and network engineering for ISPs, data centre operators and hosting providers worldwide, and builds HORA, an AI network operations platform.
